assumptions: Source definition: the scalar resistivity and conductivity refer to the same material response (9.3, Resistivity).

Application profile: passive, finite scalar bulk properties. Isotropy, or a separately justified one-dimensional scalar reduction, must make the scalar law adequate. No material, room temperature or numerical coefficient is a default.

gaps: Add S/m, ohm m and electrical_conductivity; electrical_resistivity reuses the prior definition. Neither property matches a supplied runtime meaning.
Carry material state and scalar-versus-tensor status in instantiated context. Do not alias conductivity to conductance merely because both describe electrical conduction.

models.inverse_notes: The sole inverse solves sigma given rho: sigma=1/rho, requiring finite rho>0; recovered sigma must satisfy the original sigma>0 guard. rho=0.0002 ohm m gives sigma=5000 S/m, and substitution returns 0.0002. rho=0 has no finite sigma solution, corresponding only to an infinite-conductivity limit; sigma=0 is also excluded rather than accepted by continuity. Every admissible rho determines exactly one sigma; there are no root branches. A reciprocal does not establish compatible specimen conditions or causal invertibility.
limitations: A tensor inverse is not a componentwise reciprocal. This record does not handle anisotropic tensors, complex conductivity, active negative differential response, ideal zero conductivity or infinite conductivity.
The identity contributes no empirical fit error; uncertainty comes from the material-property input and its conditions. Published rounded example pairs are not new independent measurements.

references.method: Published resistivity is retained, rather than substituting the recomputed reciprocal. Half-last-digit sigma rounding is 0.005e7 S/m; inversion changes rho by less than 1.414e-11 ohm m. Add reported-rho rounding 0.005e-8 ohm m to obtain a bound below 6.5e-11 ohm m.
references.provenance: openstax-conductivity, Table 9.1 copper at 20 degrees Celsius. Published tabular-pair oracle; origin of the table measurements and uncertainties is not specified.

references.method: Independent definition route: synthetic uniform E=0.24 V/m and J=1200 A/m^2 give sigma=J/E=5000 S/m and rho=E/J=0.0002 ohm m. Expected comes from the field/current-density ratio, not execution of 1/sigma. Exact synthetic values; tolerance covers floating-point noise only.
references.provenance: Curator derivation using the two property definitions in 9.3, Resistivity and Eq. 9.6. A stipulated passive scalar material state, not a measured material calibration.

rejection_cases.reason: An ideal insulator would have infinite resistivity; the original reciprocal denominator vanishes.
Negative differential conductivity is outside the declared passive bulk-property class.
The conductivity value is required; a material name alone is not a numerical input.

The numerator 1 is dimensionless reciprocal identity, not a physical constant or fitted coefficient; constants is therefore empty. No scale conversion is inlined. assumptions: Source approximation (OpenStax Eq. 9.10): resistance varies approximately linearly over a suitable material-specific interval. If alpha comes from resistivity, the source derivation requires negligible change of L/A.

Application requirement: document a constant effective resistance coefficient for the actual reference state, material/phase, uniform temperature, pressure and mechanical constraint. No universal numeric temperature range is asserted; the algebraic guards alone are insufficient for applicability.

Source-backed copper profile (NBS Section 1.1(b), printed p. 4): alpha_20=0.00393 K^-1 describes standard copper between material points on a freely expanding wire; cited measurements span 10–100 degrees Celsius. This is resistance, not volume-resistivity, calibration. It is not a default for arbitrary copper.
Source numerical carbon profile: Example 9.8(b) applies alpha=-0.0005 K^-1 from 20 to 60 degrees Celsius. This is illustrative use, not a measured calibration of every carbon resistor.

gaps: Add ohm, K (difference semantics), K^-1, resistance_temperature_coefficient and temperature_difference. electrical_resistance reuses batch 01.
Reference temperature, absolute state temperatures, calibration interval and mechanical response must be carried and checked in context; scalar guards cannot enforce these contextual facts.
Do not alias resistance_temperature_coefficient to a bulk-resistivity coefficient without the required geometry/constraint argument. No material coefficient is embedded as a universal constant.

models.inverse_notes: Solve R_ref given R,alpha,delta_T: R_ref=R/(1+alpha*delta_T), requiring R>0 and factor>0; 230 ohm,0.004 K^-1,-20 K recovers 250 ohm and substitution gives 230. Solve delta_T given R,R_ref,alpha: delta_T=(R/R_ref-1)/alpha, requiring R_ref>0, alpha!=0, R>0 and a recovered state in the calibrated interval; the same values recover -20 K. alpha=0 with R=R_ref leaves delta_T undetermined within the allowed interval; with R!=R_ref there is no solution. Solve alpha given R,R_ref,delta_T: alpha=(R/R_ref-1)/delta_T, requiring R_ref>0, delta_T!=0, R>0; 230,250,-20 recovers 0.004 K^-1 and substitutes correctly. delta_T=0,R=R_ref leaves alpha undetermined; delta_T=0,R!=R_ref is inconsistent. A recovered alpha=0 is allowed when delta_T!=0 and R=R_ref. A recovered delta_T=0 is allowed when alpha!=0 and R=R_ref. All nonsingular inverses are single valued, but estimating a coefficient from one pair gives no statistical validation. Original positivity and contextual interval/constraint requirements apply to every inverse. Absolute temperature cannot be inferred without T_ref.
limitations: No generic fit population, residual distribution or confidence interval is supplied by OpenStax. NBS reports specimen variation; it does not establish a uniform error bound for every resistor. Measurement, coefficient uncertainty and nonlinearity are separate contributions.

For the historical copper profile, NBS Section 1.1(b), printed p. 3 reports coefficient agreement within 0.00001 K^-1 for investigated samples above 94 percent standard conductivity. That concerns a coefficient-conductivity rule, not a resistance prediction confidence interval. It must not be propagated as a universal guarantee.

NBS discusses wider approximate copper ranges for tabulation (printed p. 4); no precise extrapolation accuracy is claimed here. The 10–100-degree-Celsius interval is a conservative documented calibration profile, not the broad mathematical domain.

Do not use this law across phase changes, large nonlinear temperature dependence or different mechanical constraints without additional evidence. delta_T=0 and alpha=0 are admissible; a predicted zero resistance is an extrapolation outside the positive-resistor profile, not evidence of superconductivity.

references.method: Published 2.94 kilohms becomes expected 2940 ohm. Conservative printed-digit rounding: R_ref +/-5 ohm, alpha +/-0.00005 K^-1, each integer endpoint temperature +/-0.5 K, and reported output +/-5 ohm. Interval extremes yield less than 17.54 ohm total comparison allowance; 18 ohm bounds this. This is a rounding check, not a fit-error allowance.

references.method: Independent linear-interpolation construction: a synthetic calibrated segment has R(290 K)=220 ohm and R(330 K)=260 ohm. At 320 K the reference value is 250 ohm and normalized slope is (1 ohm/K)/(250 ohm)=0.004 K^-1. At 300 K, one quarter of the endpoint rise gives 230 ohm. This constructs the oracle from calibration endpoints rather than evaluating the serialized expression. Exact stipulated affine data; tolerance is numerical only.
references.provenance: Curator synthetic derivation for an exactly affine passive resistor on 290–330 K. Tests cooling and reference normalization, not actual material accuracy.

references.method: Independent limiting identity: an exactly flat calibrated resistance curve has the same value at both states. Synthetic ideal temperature-insensitive interval, not a claim of exactly zero coefficient in a named real material.

rejection_cases.reason: Zero reference resistance is outside this normalized positive-resistor model.
The affine factor vanishes. This inadmissible extrapolation does not establish a zero-resistance material state.
The specimen/reference-specific coefficient cannot be inferred from the temperature difference.

relationship.translation_notes: R_ref maps to source R_0, delta_T to source Delta T, and alpha to source alpha. delta_T is a signed temperature difference in K, numerically equal to the Celsius difference, not an absolute temperature. The reference temperature remains explicit contextual metadata, not a universal 20-degree-Celsius constant. alpha has K^-1, making alpha*delta_T dimensionless; [R]=[R_ref]=M L^2 T^-3 I^-2. Literal 1 is the dimensionless baseline multiplier, not a fitted constant. Unlike a material resistivity coefficient, an effective resistance coefficient may include the declared mechanical/expansion response. This is one canonical relationship with qualified parameterizations, not a new equation for each material.

assumptions: Source definition (Eq. 9.1): charge and elapsed time refer to the same cross section and interval.

Application convention: the orientation is fixed throughout the accounting interval. Include charge moved during every part of the elapsed window; counting only active-time charge requires justification that other periods contribute zero.

The average-current quantity intentionally differs from prior electric_current (steady DC). A binding requires a proved constant-current interval or an explicit temporal adapter; unit equality is insufficient.

models.inverse_notes: Solve delta_Q given I_avg,delta_t: delta_Q=I_avg*delta_t with delta_t>0; I_avg=-2 A,delta_t=3 s gives -6 C and forward substitution gives -2 A. I_avg=0 at any known positive duration gives unique delta_Q=0. Solve delta_t given delta_Q,I_avg: delta_t=delta_Q/I_avg requires I_avg!=0 and a strictly positive recovered duration (nonzero delta_Q and I_avg must have the same sign). delta_Q=-6 C,I_avg=-2 A gives 3 s and substitutes correctly. If both charge and average are zero, all positive durations are possible; if I_avg=0 with nonzero charge, no finite duration works. If charge is zero with nonzero average, the algebraic result delta_t=0 violates the original domain. Each admissible nonsingular inverse is single valued; no root choice. No reconstruction of a waveform or instantaneous current is possible from this scalar average alone.
limitations: An average alone does not provide instantaneous current, peak current, RMS current, heating or power. Equal units do not authorize binding it to an instantaneous-current input.

An interval of zero duration is undefined. A zero net transfer can result from cancellation, so it does not imply zero energy dissipation. This record supplies no transient evolution, circuit solution or safety guidance.

references.method: Published expected 180 A is retained. The displayed classroom values are evaluated as nominal exact numbers, giving an exact quotient; 1e-10 A permits floating-point noise. This is a textbook arithmetic oracle, not an assertion of measured-input precision or physical uncertainty.

references.method: Independent unit-count construction: in each of three one-second bins, two one-coulomb packets cross opposite the positive orientation. Each bin has -2 C/s and their duration-weighted mean is -2 A. Total transfer is -6 C. Synthetic exact packets, not an electron-count experiment; tolerance is numerical only.
references.provenance: Curator independent counting derivation from the ampere definition in Eq. 9.2.

references.method: Limiting identity: no net transferred charge over a positive window has zero signed average. Synthetic boundary; does not assert that instantaneous current was always zero.
references.provenance: Curator definitional boundary check; numerical-only tolerance.

rejection_cases.reason: A zero-duration averaging window is undefined, including when transferred charge is also zero.
Duration is defined as positive elapsed time; reverse charge orientation rather than using negative duration.
Transferred charge alone does not identify the averaging duration.

relationship.translation_notes: Local I_avg maps to source I_ave, delta_Q to Delta Q and delta_t to Delta t. Q denotes net charge transported across a chosen section, not the change of charge stored in an unrelated component. C=A*s; division by s gives A, dimension I. No conversion coefficient occurs. Positive orientation is arbitrary but consistent for transferred charge and current; negative values reverse it. Use a new interval-average quantity ID rather than silently binding to the batch-01 steady-current ports. The definition is broader than DC, while the assignment uses its DC-compatible average interpretation without adding a transient solver.

sources.evidence: Average current divides net transported charge by elapsed time. The published starter example reports 180 A; the section distinguishes instantaneous current.
